lessons.title: Model and testing lab: a tiny search core
lessons.summary: Build a pure Swift package that preserves value semantics and meaningful failure states, then prove its behavior with deterministic tests.
objectives: Implement a small value model, state enum, protocol, and synchronous boundary.
Write tests for behavior that matters rather than merely mirroring code structure.
Use Swift Testing syntax and recognize the XCTest counterpart.
Document what a host-only model test verifies and what it leaves untested.

sections.title: Build a core small enough to reason about
sections.html:
You have probably tested a Kotlin reducer or ViewModel by replacing its repository with a fake. Today we recreate the smallest useful version of that workflow in Swift: a search draft, a finite state model, a service contract, and a pure synchronous load function. There is no screen, network, persistence, actor, or dependency container. Each extra concern would make it harder to tell whether a failure belongs to syntax, state semantics, or infrastructure.

The product rules are concrete. A draft edit must not mutate the original. An absent procedure remains absent rather than becoming a sentinel ID. A missing specialty requires a choice. A successful query with no results remains successful. An offline service failure produces a retry state. A successful nonempty response preserves its names.

Use synthetic names and identifiers throughout. The production cancellation feature supplies examples of model and test organization; we are not importing its data or claiming to reproduce its business rules. Reading the worked solution is useful reference material, but it does not pre-complete your exercise. Save predictions first and compare them with the tests you run.

Plan about twenty minutes for modeling, twenty for test construction, twenty for implementation, and the remaining time for explaining failures and documenting limits. The lab can also be completed on paper with predicted test outcomes if a compatible toolchain is unavailable.

sections.title: Set up one module and one test target
sections.html:
In your own scratch directory, use the Sources/FoundationLab and Tests/FoundationLabTests layout from session 005. For this modern Swift Testing example, use the following manifest with a Swift 6.0-or-newer toolchain. The authoring machine has Swift 6.4. This deliberately selects a modern lab baseline without changing the client graph's mixed settings.

// swift-tools-version: 6.0
import PackageDescription

let package = Package(
    name: "FoundationLab",
    products: [
        .library(name: "FoundationLab", targets: ["FoundationLab"])
    ],
    targets: [
        .target(name: "FoundationLab"),
        .testTarget(
            name: "FoundationLabTests",
            dependencies: ["FoundationLab"]
        )
    ]
)

The manifest has no remote dependency. Its library can compile on the host because we use only ordinary Swift types. Put the model and load function under the library target, and put test imports and fakes under the test target. swift test is run from this scratch package, not from the full client root.

The test framework is named Testing, while your application module is FoundationLab. @testable import FoundationLab allows the test target to access internal declarations when the module is built with testing enabled. It does not expose private implementation everywhere or turn internal types into public API. A test target dependency and a module import are both needed; one does not replace the other.

sections.title: Write invariants before choosing implementations
sections.html:
Declare SearchDraft as a struct with optional Int64 identifiers and a query string. Its computed displayQuery returns All providers only for an empty query. This is a presentation rule, not a mutation of the underlying string. State the behavior for nil identifiers separately: the absence of a procedure is allowed, while the absence of a specialty blocks a search.

Declare LabSearchState with idle, loading, loaded(providers:), and failed(message:). The state vocabulary includes situations a future UI may use, even though this synchronous function returns only a terminal loaded or failed state. Do not insert a transient loading state into a return value just to exercise all enum cases. A later asynchronous owner would publish transitions.

The protocol has one operation: search(for draft: SearchDraft) throws -> [String]. The external label for reads naturally at the call; draft is the local parameter name. Passing the draft by value makes the service boundary explicit. It does not stop a conforming class from managing its own internal state.

Make the fake configurable with Result. A successful empty array and an offline error then require different fixture constructors. This is more honest than a fake with one Boolean whose meaning changes between tests. Keep the fake in the test target unless it serves a real runtime purpose. Avoid designing a reusable mocking framework before the first behavior is proven.

sections.title: A worked core, with explicit failure mapping
sections.html:
Try your implementation first, then compare it with this complete library source. All declarations are internal by default, which is sufficient for this package's tests. No Foundation or UI import is needed.

struct SearchDraft: Equatable {
    var specialtyID: Int64?
    var procedureID: Int64?
    var query: String

    var displayQuery: String {
        query.isEmpty ? "All providers" : query
    }
}

enum LabSearchState: Equatable {
    case idle
    case loading
    case loaded(providers: [String])
    case failed(message: String)
}

enum LabSearchError: Error { case offline }

protocol LabProviderServing {
    func search(for draft: SearchDraft) throws -> [String]
}

func load(
    draft: SearchDraft,
    service: any LabProviderServing
) -> LabSearchState {
    guard draft.specialtyID != nil else {
        return .failed(message: "Choose a specialty")
    }
    do {
        return .loaded(providers: try service.search(for: draft))
    } catch LabSearchError.offline {
        return .failed(message: "Offline: retry")
    } catch {
        return .failed(message: "Unable to search")
    }
}

The guard checks the specialty requirement before calling the service. It checks absence rather than rejecting a numeric sentinel. The do block produces loaded even when the returned array is empty. The first catch maps the known offline case to retry guidance; the final catch supplies a generic unexpected-failure message.

This small boundary intentionally turns service errors into presentation states. In production you might retain a typed failure, expose a retry policy, or report an error through an observability boundary. A generic message should not be your only diagnostic evidence in a real app. Here, synchronous deterministic mapping isolates the distinction we want to learn.

Neither this function nor the protocol implements thread safety, request cancellation, input trimming, localization, caching, or result ordering. Those are future requirements. A model test is most useful when it makes its scope explicit instead of implying that a passing assertion covers unimplemented concerns.

sections.title: Read Swift Testing and recognize XCTest
sections.html:
Swift Testing discovers functions annotated with @Test. #expect records a condition and useful diagnostics when it is false. These are macros provided by the Testing module, not comments or preprocessor directives. A suite can group tests, and parameterized tests can run one behavior over several fixtures. The active cancellation tests already use this framework.

XCTest is also widely used, including for UI automation and older tests. An XCTest unit test conventionally subclasses XCTestCase and defines methods beginning with test; assertions such as XCTAssertEqual express expectations. This optional alternative belongs in a test target that has the lab module available:

import XCTest
@testable import FoundationLab

final class SearchDraftXCTests: XCTestCase {
    func testDisplayQueryForEmptyInput() {
        let draft = SearchDraft(
            specialtyID: 10, procedureID: nil, query: ""
        )
        XCTAssertEqual(draft.displayQuery, "All providers")
    }
}

Choose the framework already used by the target and the behavior you need. Do not mix XCTest assertion APIs inside a Swift Testing test and assume identical failure reporting. The two frameworks can coexist in a test target, but that is not a reason to duplicate every assertion.

Keep each test's fixtures local. Swift Testing can execute tests in parallel, so shared mutable globals turn a simple value-model test into an order-dependent exercise. Avoid sleeps: the core is synchronous and needs none. A fake gives controlled results directly.

sections.title: Prove the product distinctions and learn from a red test
sections.html:
The worked tests below belong to Tests/FoundationLabTests. They assert behavior at the boundary: original value preservation, correct fallback, empty success versus offline failure, missing-specialty validation, and preservation of a nonempty response. They do not assert that your implementation uses a particular number of branches.

import Testing
@testable import FoundationLab

struct FakeLabService: LabProviderServing {
    let result: Result<[String], LabSearchError>
    func search(for draft: SearchDraft) throws -> [String] {
        try result.get()
    }
}

@Test func editingPreservesOriginal() {
    let original = SearchDraft(
        specialtyID: 10, procedureID: nil, query: ""
    )
    var edited = original
    edited.specialtyID = 20
    #expect(original.specialtyID == 10)
    #expect(edited.specialtyID == 20)
    #expect(original.procedureID == nil)
    #expect(original.displayQuery == "All providers")
}

@Test func successfulEmptyAndFailureRemainDistinct() {
    let draft = SearchDraft(
        specialtyID: 10, procedureID: nil, query: "Ada"
    )
    let empty = load(
        draft: draft, service: FakeLabService(result: .success([]))
    )
    let offline = load(
        draft: draft, service: FakeLabService(result: .failure(.offline))
    )
    #expect(empty == .loaded(providers: []))
    #expect(offline == .failed(message: "Offline: retry"))
    #expect(empty != offline)
}

@Test func missingSpecialtyRequiresAChoice() {
    let draft = SearchDraft(
        specialtyID: nil, procedureID: nil, query: ""
    )
    let state = load(
        draft: draft,
        service: FakeLabService(result: .success(["Dr. Ada"]))
    )
    #expect(state == .failed(message: "Choose a specialty"))
}

@Test func nonemptySuccessKeepsNames() {
    let draft = SearchDraft(
        specialtyID: 10, procedureID: nil, query: "Ada"
    )
    let state = load(
        draft: draft,
        service: FakeLabService(result: .success(["Dr. Ada"]))
    )
    #expect(state == .loaded(providers: ["Dr. Ada"]))
}

The first test would catch accidental reference semantics in a mutable model. The second would catch replacing errors with empty arrays. The third would catch omission of the validation rule, and the fourth protects nonempty success. A failure should lead to an explanation of which product fact was violated, not simply a change to the expected string until everything turns green.

As a diagnostic exercise, temporarily replace the do/catch implementation with .loaded(providers: (try? service.search(for: draft)) ?? []). Predict which assertion fails before running. Restore the explicit error mapping afterward. This controlled mutation shows that the failure-distinction test protects something real.

Open the active booking-prompt tests at their repository anchor. They use descriptive Test labels, locally constructed responses, and parameterized inputs for business variants. Copy the discipline of controlled fixtures and named behavior, not the domain-specific cancellation codes. Their inclusion is confirmed by the cancellation test source glob.

A test asserting empty success and offline yield distinct expected states.
A test counting lines in the implementation.
quiz.explanation: The test protects a product distinction at the boundary. Importing or measuring code cannot show that retry information survived.

quiz.question: What does @testable import FoundationLab provide?
options: Access to internal declarations when built for testing, without making all private details public.
Automatic production dependency injection.
A guarantee that UIKit works on a host-only target.
quiz.explanation: Testable import changes test access to internal module declarations with testing enabled. It does not change platform APIs or install dependencies.

quiz.question: Why keep fake configuration and fixtures local to each Swift Testing test?
options: Because structs cannot be global.
Because parallel tests should not interfere through shared mutable state.
Because Swift Testing prohibits all reusable helpers.
quiz.explanation: Parallel execution can expose shared mutable fixture races and order dependence. Reusable pure helpers are fine; local ownership keeps each case deterministic.

quiz.question: What does a passing swift test for this lab establish?
options: The iOS app is signed, accessible, and ready to release.
The tested pure model behaviors work in this host-compatible package.
All production service implementations conform correctly at runtime.
quiz.explanation: Scope matters. The lab checks its own core and fixtures; app integration, platforms, UI, and networking still require their respective verification.

sections.title: Recall first, check second, explain the mismatch
sections.html:
An experienced Android engineer can understand a Swift explanation quickly while still reaching for Kotlin semantics under pressure. Retrieval practice catches that gap. Today you will predict small programs, explain mistakes, and walk one real feature from model to callback to target. The goal is transferable reasoning, not memorizing spellings or declaring the whole platform mastered.

Close the earlier lesson text for the first pass. Write answers with confidence marks: certain, tentative, or guessing. Then check the worked explanations and run the isolated snippets if you have the toolchain. When a prediction changes, write the assumption that misled you. For example, replacing val with let is easy; remembering that a struct bound to let cannot mutate a stored field is a different skill.

Use three columns in your notes: observation, language rule, and product consequence. An array is empty is an observation; successful data is not an error is a domain distinction; show no matches rather than retry is a product consequence. This format prevents correct-looking syntax from substituting for a correct explanation.

Keep unfinished exercises pending. Instructor examples and your own practice remain separate evidence.

sections.title: Predict binding, aliasing, and absence
sections.html:
Before running the following standalone program, predict the three printed values. Explain which assignment creates independent value state, which property still shares a class instance, and why the fallback is not used for the empty query. Then say whether changing first.query would compile.

final class ReviewNotes { var text = "Initial" }
struct ReviewDraft {
    var query: String
    var specialtyID: Int64?
    let notes: ReviewNotes
}

let first = ReviewDraft(
    query: "", specialtyID: nil, notes: ReviewNotes()
)
var edited = first
edited.query = "Ada"
edited.notes.text = "Shared"
print(first.query.isEmpty)
print(first.notes.text)
let optionalQuery: String? = first.query
print(optionalQuery ?? "Fallback")
Worked prediction — open after answering

The outputs are true, Shared, and a blank line. The outer struct values have independent query fields, but both contain the same Notes reference. A present empty string is not nil, so nil coalescing preserves it. Changing first.query fails because first is a let-bound struct; editing the nested class does not replace the struct's stored reference.

Now retrieve the syntax distinctions without checking session 001. What external label is used for func subtitle(for draft: ReviewDraft)? Why might a wire identifier use Int64 rather than Int? What extra contract does Hashable provide beyond Equatable? Does String.count mean the same thing as Kotlin String.length for every Unicode input?

Explain each answer with a concrete consequence. Argument labels affect call sites; integer width affects data contracts; hashing affects collections rather than identity; text representation affects length limits. Facts become useful when you can name the bug they prevent.

sections.title: Recover the state model instead of patching booleans
sections.html:
On a blank page, declare a state with idle, loading, loaded names, and failed message. Write a title function without default. Give one output for successful empty results and one for offline failure. Then add a hypothetical offline case and identify every consumer you would expect the compiler to revisit.

Worked reasoning — open after drafting

An associated-value enum stores names only in loaded and an error description only in failed. An exhaustive switch exposes missing handling when a new local case is introduced. Empty loaded results should express no matches; idle should express a search not yet begun; failure should retain enough meaning to offer recovery. The enum controls representable combinations, while a separate owner still controls valid transitions.

For a second retrieval task, compare case failed(message: String) with enum Reason: String. Which data varies per instance? What happens when a raw-value initializer receives a newly introduced server string? Do not answer by saying both are enums; describe the different boundary behavior.

A good answer notes that associated data varies for each construction and a raw value is fixed for each case. Unknown raw input yields nil, requiring a compatibility decision. Neither form automatically validates message contents or becomes Codable just because it has strings.

Finally, consider a requirement to preserve old results while loading new ones. Our simple four-state model cannot express that directly. You could add a loading payload, nest a request status inside a content model, or define another appropriate state. Identify the product rule first. Retrieval includes knowing when a previously useful model has reached its limit.

sections.title: Audit service substitution, dispatch, and lost errors
sections.html:
Explain a consumer taking any ProviderServing without saying every conformer is a class. What makes a synchronous fake replaceable? Which parts of the protocol signature must align? What would need to change if the contract becomes async? Answer these before opening the source anchors.

Next, audit the expression (try? service.providers()) ?? []. It is valid Swift, so a compiler will not reject the product mistake. Name two originally distinct outcomes and the UI affordance lost after the transformation. Then rewrite the boundary with do/catch or a typed result so that empty success and failure remain distinct.

Worked contract and failure explanation

A conformer satisfies the required operation's name, labels, types, and effects. The existential hides the concrete type, which can be a value or reference. Ordinary throws requires explicit try at the call. Async adds suspension to the contract rather than merely decorating an implementation. The optional fallback erases the error and makes offline look like zero matches, losing retry meaning.

Now retrieve extension dispatch: a method is supplied only in a protocol extension, and the conformer declares a same-named method. Through a protocol-typed value, the helper is selected from the extension. If conformer-specific behavior is part of the contract, declare it as a requirement and optionally provide a default implementation. Being able to say this precisely prevents a fake passing while production silently takes a different helper.

Finally, define escaping without mentioning threads. A stored plain closure parameter must be marked escaping because it can outlive the call. That annotation does not make it weak, Sendable, asynchronous, or guaranteed to run. Those are separate reviews.

sections.title: Draw the stored callback and nested-work graphs
sections.html:
Draw an owner holding a callback that strongly captures the owner. Remove the external variable and mark which edges remain. Predict whether deinit can break the loop by clearing the callback. Then redraw the graph with weak capture and explain what a separately saved callback can do after the owner disappears.

Worked ownership explanation

The owner-to-callback and callback-to-owner strong edges keep the cycle alive. Deinit cannot remove a loop that prevents deallocation. Weak capture removes the callback's owning edge; a saved callback can remain alive while its captured owner becomes nil. Its body needs a deliberate absent-owner path. Optional callback invocation and optional owner unwrapping solve different absence cases.

For a harder question, the weak callback performs guard let self and creates another stored closure using self. Label the inner capture. Explain why the outer capture policy does not automatically apply to the nested closure. If the stored work is cleared after execution, what distinguishes temporary retention from an unbounded leak?

The guard introduces a strong local owner. The inner closure can retain that binding until its own lifetime ends. You must inspect who stores the inner work and when it releases it. A guaranteed release path can make retention appropriate; a new cycle or a never-completing operation can keep resources alive unexpectedly.

Choose unowned only from a proven lifetime relationship. Do not propose it merely because a callback is normally fast. Also separate memory lifetime from lifecycle policy: a callback that safely finds a screen alive may still be semantically wrong to update after dismissal. Ownership safety does not decide cancellation or UI validity.

sections.title: Classify the failure before touching the build
sections.html:
You are told that the machine has Swift 6.4, ZDAppointments starts with tools 5.9, its minimum iOS version is 17, and another target explicitly sets SWIFT_VERSION to 6. Explain why none of these facts contradicts the others. Then name the evidence needed to know the failing target's effective language mode rather than borrowing a neighboring target's setting.

The installed compiler, manifest tools requirement, source language mode, and deployment target are separate. Effective build settings for the chosen target and route settle the mode; the newest compiler version alone does not. An SDK can contain APIs unavailable on the minimum supported runtime, so availability also requires explicit reasoning.

Classify three failures: a type does not conform to a protocol; a module cannot be imported; and a test compiles but never runs. The first suggests signature or requirement checking. The second suggests dependency, product exposure, platform, or source membership. The third suggests discovery conventions, test target inclusion, or the scheme's test action. These categories tell you what to inspect next.

Retrieve the Xcode vocabulary: target is a component; configuration is a build-setting set; scheme plans actions using components; destination chooses a runtime or platform; workspace groups the project graph. A generated Project.swift is not app runtime code just because both use Swift.

For the pure model lab, host swift test is appropriate. For a UIKit test, a suitable iOS destination is needed. A source-only type check, a passing package test, and a successful simulator app build are different evidence. Write the exact verification scope beside each claim.

sections.title: Walk one active feature in six observations
sections.html:
Follow the repository anchors without editing source. Start at the question model and its optional subtitle. Follow its computed wrapper to NavigationState and the switch extracting question data. Locate the stored submission closure and escaping initializer. Trace the weak controller callback and coordinator's nested Task. Finish at the source and test globs in Project.swift.

Record an observed line and a justified conclusion at each stop. A source glob proves membership, not successful compilation. Weak capture proves a nonowning edge, not cancellation. The booking-prompt tests connect Testing macros and locally constructed fixtures to business variants; your host-only lab does not replace their platform integration.

Readiness means explaining this chain and implementing a changed example independently. Choose focused practice from your weak spots: three assignment predictions, an added enum case, two error fixtures, or one ownership graph. Revisit it in two days and a week with changed inputs so that you retrieve the rule rather than memorize output.

quiz.question: A copied struct contains a mutable class reference. Which prediction is correct?
options: All nested state is automatically cloned.
The struct's direct fields have value semantics, but the contained class may remain shared.
All fields must be immutable because structs are values.
quiz.explanation: Value assignment preserves the outer value model. It copies a class reference as a reference, not as a recursively cloned object.

quiz.question: A weak callback unwraps self before creating an inner Task that uses self. What can you conclude?
options: The Task must also capture weakly.
The inner work can retain the strong local binding; storage and completion need separate inspection.
A permanent leak is proven without more context.
quiz.explanation: Each closure has its own captures. Strong inner retention is evidence of lifetime, not by itself evidence of an unbreakable cycle or cancellation behavior.

quiz.question: The installed compiler is Swift 6.4. Does every client target necessarily use Swift 6 language mode?
options: Yes, compiler and language mode are identical.
No; inspect effective settings and manifests for the selected target.
Only if its deployment target is iOS 17.
quiz.explanation: The compiler can support compatibility modes. Tools requirements and OS deployment values do not settle a target's source mode by themselves.

quiz.question: A renderer uses default for a local state enum. What review question matters when a case is added?
options: Whether the new product behavior is being silently grouped instead of explicitly considered.
Whether Swift switches need a Java-style break.
Whether the case name should be converted to a raw string.
quiz.explanation: A default can conceal omitted behavior. For locally owned finite states, explicit handling makes added product decisions visible.

exercise.solution:
This complete standalone implementation uses a weak callback because refresh may be retained after the owner is gone. The fake is a struct; the owner is a class because the exercise intentionally needs reference lifetime. Read it only after drafting your version.

enum ReviewOutcome: Equatable {
    case idle
    case loaded([String])
    case failed(String)
}
enum ReviewFailure: Error { case offline }
protocol ReviewServing {
    func names() throws -> [String]
}
struct ReviewFake: ReviewServing {
    let result: Result<[String], ReviewFailure>
    func names() throws -> [String] { try result.get() }
}
final class ReviewOwner {
    var state: ReviewOutcome = .idle
    var refreshCallback: (() -> Void)?
    let service: any ReviewServing

    init(service: any ReviewServing) {
        self.service = service
        refreshCallback = { [weak self] in
            guard let self else { return }
            do {
                self.state = .loaded(try self.service.names())
            } catch {
                self.state = .failed("Retry")
            }
        }
    }
}
func summary(of state: ReviewOutcome) -> String {
    switch state {
    case .idle: return "Start"
    case let .loaded(names):
        return names.isEmpty ? "No matches" : "\(names.count) providers"
    case let .failed(message): return message
    }
}
func inspectReviewOwner() {
    var owner: ReviewOwner? = ReviewOwner(
        service: ReviewFake(result: .success([]))
    )
    let saved = owner?.refreshCallback
    weak var probe = owner
    saved?()
    if let state = owner?.state {
